summary: Offers advice on how to host a successful IETF Birds-of-a-Feather session, particularly one aimed at forming a working group, based on the experience of the authors with many BOFs that worked or failed. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5434 gives advice for organizing an IETF Birds-of-a-Feather session, especially when the goal is to form a working group. It emphasizes understanding the problem and building community agreement before the meeting.

questions: how to run a successful ietf bof
how to form an ietf working group
do you need a bof to form a working group
how do you prepare for an ietf bof
subtitle: Practical advice for preparing, running, and following up an IETF BOF

tldr.problem: A Birds-of-a-Feather session can fail when organizers start late, lack agreement on the problem, or use the meeting to debate solutions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5434 recommends early public discussion, a clear problem statement and charter, focused questions, and follow-up with Area Directors.
tldr.outcome: The Informational memo offers guidance, not process rules. It notes that a BOF is not formally required before forming a working group.

facts.label: Recommended preparation
facts.value: Begin 3 to 4 months before the meeting

facts.label: Process requirement
facts.value: A BOF is not required before forming a working group

today: RFC 5434 is an Informational guide published in February 2009. The supplied metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it describes advice rather than required process.

sections.title: What a BOF Should Establish
sections.content:
A Birds-of-a-Feather (BOF) session can be a one-time discussion or a step toward forming an IETF working group. When the goal is a group, the session should show that the IETF is the right place to solve a real problem and that enough people will do the work.

Attendees also need to agree on the work's scope, expected documents, and a reasonable chance of completing them. The RFC presents its recommendations as an ideal process based on experience with earlier BOFs.
sections.plainLanguage: A BOF can test whether the community should form a working group. Participants need to agree on the problem, the work, and who will help.

sections.title: Prepare Through Public Discussion
sections.content:
The RFC recommends starting with a small group that writes a problem statement and checks whether existing work already covers it. Organizers should consult relevant working groups and Area Directors, then create a public mailing list and invite broader participation.

Discussion should focus first on the problem, not competing solutions. Organizers should circulate a proposed charter and the questions for the BOF before the meeting. Since the scheduling request deadline is about six weeks before an IETF meeting, the RFC recommends beginning preparation several months earlier.
sections.plainLanguage: Start early, invite public discussion, and agree on the problem before debating solutions. Share the charter and meeting questions in advance.

sections.title: Understand the Problem Before Solutions
sections.content:
The RFC says working-group output is useful only when it addresses a real problem faced by customers, operators, or deployers. Those people are often best placed to explain the difficulty and the requirements for a solution.

Debates about competing technologies can hide disagreement about the problem itself. A clear, shared problem statement gives the group a basis for judging whether an approach is suitable.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask the people who face the problem to explain it. A shared description helps the group assess proposed solutions.

sections.title: Run the Meeting and Follow Up
sections.content:
Organizers should keep the agenda focused on whether the IETF should form a working group with the proposed charter. Questions can test whether the problem is clear and solvable, whether the charter has support, and whether people will review or edit documents.

After the BOF, organizers should assess the result with the Area Directors and decide whether to finalize a charter or do more work. The RFC notes that a second BOF has higher expectations and should resolve issues raised at the first.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the meeting to find out whether the group and charter have support. Afterward, review unresolved issues with the Area Directors.

sections.title: Common Pitfalls and the Role of a BOF
sections.content:
Common pitfalls include starting late, advertising poorly, spending too much time on solutions, asking unclear questions, and allowing presentations to distract from the purpose of the session. Organizers should also not assume they will chair the BOF or any future working group.

The RFC states that no process rule requires a BOF before a working group forms. The formal requirement is approval of a charter by the IESG with the sponsoring Area Director or Directors; a BOF is one way to engage the community and develop that charter.
sections.plainLanguage: A BOF is useful for discussion, but it is not a formal requirement for forming a working group. Clear preparation helps avoid delays and unfocused debate.

references.text: Bradner, S., "IETF Working Group Guidelines and Procedures", BCP 25, RFC 2418, September 1998.
